newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia meets IMF obligations - offical.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia meets IMF obligations - offical.

text.p: Yugoslavia has met all the conditions set by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for restoring its membership in the organisation, a senior government official said on Thursday.

"Yugoslavia has accepted a quota set by the IMF and the obligation to settle its due liabilities," federal Finance Minister Tomica Raicevic said. "Parliament's endorsment of government's activities today was also one of the conditions set by the IMF."
Raicevic said it was now up to the IMF board of directors to decide to admit Yugoslavia.
Yugoslavia accepted a quota of 36.52 percent of the assets and liabilities of the former Yugoslavia in the Fund. It also accepted to pay back its outstanding debt of $104 million.
But Raicevic warned that Yugoslavia has accepted the quota only in the case of the IMF and should not be confused with a future distribution of the assets of former Yugoslavia as a whole.
"We do not renounce our stands regarding international legal personality and continuity," Raicevic said.

Yugoslavia's membership in the IMF has been a cause of major dispute among politicians in Serbia. Hardliners have demanded Belgrade be given the rights of the old Yugoslav federation as its successor state, while moderates have urged a prudent and pragmatic approach.
The dispute led to the ousting in May of popular National Bank governor Dragoslav Avramovic who championed the latter.
But facing an economic disaster at home without fresh foreign capital, the Yugoslav government appears to have backed down and accepted the IMF's conditions for membership.
The Yugoslav parliament on Thursday endorsed the federal government's activity for a speedy return to and normalisation of relations with the IMF and other financial organisations.

"Yugoslavia's reintegration to the world's financial community is an important precondition for our faster economic revival and removal of serious consequences of international sanctions imposed by the United Nations," the parliament said.
It also "expects the IMF to take into account the relevant factors and to give special attention to the effects of the sanctions when assessing Yugoslavia's capability to fulfil the IMF commitments".

Yugoslavia's economy has been crippled by wars in Croatia and Bosnia, disintegration of the single Yugoslav market and a three-year U.N. trade embargo to punish Belgrade for its support of Bosnian Serbs.

Most of the embargo was suspended after Belgrade signed the Dayton peace accord for Bosnia last November, but parts which prohibits Belgrade's access to the international financial markets remained in place.
